input:
The staffing ramp for the upgrade project is set at 19%, and it is this figure, rather than the lower alternative also put forward, that this section defends. The case for the figure rests on the shape of the work the upgrade project has to carry out, rather than on its sheer total volume. The heaviest demands arrive early, when design and procurement run alongside one another competing for many of the same people, and a ramp set below the load curve would leave posts unfilled in exactly the weeks when delay is hardest to recover. The steering group is asked to hold the figure at the level the load curve sets, rather than trimming it toward the alternative.

The monetary consequences stand in the cost table of the Costs section and are not repeated here. What the figure purchases can be stated in staffing terms alone: cover for the peak, recruited early enough to be genuinely useful when the peak arrives. A lower ramp would save against the table but pay in slippage against the programme, and that exchange remains poor while the early load stands as currently drawn, a matter the forthcoming programme revision has yet to confirm or revise
